analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer loans at each borrower's home state maximum.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act so that interest rates and fees on consumer loans — credit cards, payday loans, installment loans, and similar credit, but not home mortgages — could not exceed the maximum rate allowed by the state where the borrower lives. Today, lenders can "export" rates from states with no interest cap into states that have strict caps, so a borrower in a capped state can be charged an uncapped rate through a bank partner in another state. The bill would end that practice and restore each state's rate limit for its own residents.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states with interest-rate caps, who could no longer be charged rates above their state's limit through out-of-state bank partners. People using payday loans, high-fee installment loans, and credit cards would see rates and fees brought down to their state's maximum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes interest rates and fees on consumer credit (other than home mortgages) subject to the maximum rate permitted by the borrower's home state, reversing the practice of lenders charging rates imported from states with no cap.
Because the cap applies to 'any consumer credit transaction' and includes 'any fees associated with such a transaction,' payday lenders could not sidestep rate limits by relabeling interest as fees.

analysis.who_pays: High-rate consumer lenders: payday lenders, installment lenders, banks that lend across state lines at uncapped rates, and credit card issuers charging rates above certain states' caps would lose the ability to charge borrowers more than their home state allows.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and high-rate credit issuers

drawbacks.text: Rate caps can reduce access to credit: lenders who cannot charge enough to cover the risk may decline loans to borrowers with poor credit, leaving some people with no formal borrowing option at all. Opponents of rate caps typically argue this; the bill text does not include an access provision.

The bill's effect varies by state: it simply defers to each state's law, so consumers in states with no interest-rate cap would see no change, and the protection is only as strong as each state's own law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in the many states with rate caps, the bill would directly cut the cost of the most expensive consumer credit by closing the exportation loophole, and the fee-inclusion language blocks easy workarounds. The real cost is the tradeoff every rate cap carries: some borrowers with poor credit may lose access to certain loans and be pushed toward fewer options. The bill left that balance entirely to each state, which is a defensible design but means the strongest protections depend on state law rather than a national floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing ever happened to it there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island introduced the bill on September 26, 2017, joined by four cosponsors: Senators Warren, Reed, Merkley, and Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the standard first step for a Senate bill.
The action history shows no further steps: the Finance Committee never took up the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-rate consumer lenders came out ahead: payday lenders, installment lenders, and banks that lend across state lines at uncapped rates kept the ability to charge borrowers more than their home state's rate cap, because the bill died without any committee action or vote.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply each state's interest-rate cap to consumer loans made to its residents.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Jack Reed, Jeff Merkley, and Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senators (MA, RI, OR, VT), cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further action was recorded.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remaining 15 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, and the record shows no Republican support or opposition — the bill simply never moved past referral in a committee chaired by the other party.

industries.note: These lenders charge triple-digit effective rates, often through out-of-state bank partners, in states that cap rates. The bill would apply the borrower's home state cap, including fees, directly cutting their revenue in capped states.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer-lending banks
industries.note: Banks and card issuers currently rely on exporting rates from their home states, several of which have no cap, to charge cardholders above the caps in the borrower's state. The bill would make the borrower's state cap govern, limiting card and consumer-loan pricing.

industries.industry: Bank partners that rent out their charters to fintech lenders
industries.note: A growing business model pairs a nationally chartered bank with an online lender so the loan is legally made in the bank's uncapped home state. Applying the borrower's home state cap to the transaction undermines this model.

Most would pay less on loans they get, but some lenders may stop lending to the riskiest borrowers in capped states, reducing access to emergency credit. The bill gives states, not a national rule, control over where that line falls.
